Lokesh, you're furious with your friend for forgetting your birthday. Let your Binita Nani tell you about my brother Tapan. When my first baby came, Tapan drove through the night from Siliguri with a box of mangoes and sat with me for three days. That was Tapan. And the same Tapan missed my wedding reception because he was watching a football final. Also Tapan.

For years I kept flipping. Some days he was a saint; other days I swore I'd never speak to him again. It was exhausting, like a see-saw.

Then my mother told me, "Binu, he is both. Hold both in your hands." So I did. When he forgot things, I told him straight: "That hurt." And I still ate his mangoes. We never had a big explosion again. He died last year, and I miss both of him.

In the Lucknow colony cricket match, Wasim dropped an easy catch, and Sachin yelled, "Butterfingers! You're useless!" Wasim walked off without finishing the game.

That night Sachin couldn't sleep. The next afternoon he knocked on Wasim's door holding his newest comic, the one about the space pirates, which he hadn't even read yet. "Here. You can keep it," he said, looking at the doormat, and started talking about the pirates' spaceship.

Wasim took the comic but stayed in the doorway.

Wasim's Ammi, passing with a tray, said, "Sachin beta, a comic is nice. But did you tell him what it's for?"

Sachin's ears went hot. "Sorry for saying useless," he mumbled. "You're not."

Wasim opened the door wider. "Come in, then. We'll read it together."

qa.a: Sachin yelled, "Butterfingers! You're useless!"

qa.q: Why couldn't Sachin sleep that night?
qa.a: Sachin felt guilty about calling Wasim useless, and the comic was his way of trying to cancel it.

qa.q: What did the question from Wasim's Ammi help Sachin do?
qa.a: It nudged Sachin to say an actual sorry, which finished the repair the comic had only started.

qa.q: What was Wasim thinking while standing in the doorway?
qa.a: Wasim was probably still hurt and unsure, not ready to let a gift wipe away "useless" without words.

grounding: Shows a boy who gives a friend a comic after calling him useless, and a gentle question that leads to a real apology.

Saturday

I shouted at Mummy this morning. She asked, for the third time, if I'd finished my project, and I yelled, "Just leave me alone! You're always nagging!" and slammed the door. Her face.

So this afternoon I cleaned the whole flat. Swept, mopped, even the fan blades. Folded the laundry. Made her ginger tea exactly how she likes it and left it on the table. Didn't say anything. Just kept doing things.

She said "thank you", but quietly, and her eyes looked tired.

Wasim called and I told him. He said, "Bro, you cleaned the fan blades? You must feel terrible. Did you actually say sorry though?"

No. I didn't. It felt easier to mop than to say it.

Tomorrow at breakfast. Two words. Sorry, Mummy.

Jomon

qa.q: What did Jomon make for Mummy?
qa.a: Jomon made her ginger tea exactly how she likes it.

qa.q: Why did cleaning feel easier to Jomon than saying sorry?
qa.a: Jomon felt guilty and ashamed about yelling, and doing chores let him show it without facing the harder words.

qa.q: What is the wise next step in Jomon's plan?
qa.a: Saying "Sorry, Mummy" at breakfast, which names the harm the cleaning could only hint at.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel seeing the clean flat and the tea?
qa.a: Mummy may feel touched but still hurt and tired, since "you're always nagging" hasn't been taken back.

grounding: A teenage boy's diary shows him cleaning the flat and making tea after yelling at his mother, without yet saying sorry.

Sangeeta had shouted at her mother the night before, in front of the neighbours: "You don't understand anything! I'm not a child!" It was about going to the fair in Nandurbar with her friends. Sunaina had gone silent and turned to the stove.

Before dawn, Sangeeta was up. She fetched four pots of water from the well. She swept the courtyard, cleaned the cowshed, and had the chai boiling before Sunaina woke. She put the cup in her mother's hands and went to scrub the steps, saying nothing.

Sunaina watched her for a while, then called her over. "This is a lot of work for one shout," she said. "The tea is good. But I'd like to hear it too."

Sangeeta looked at the wet broom. "Sorry, Aai. I didn't mean you don't understand." Sunaina nodded and handed her half the chai.

Jahnavi, you asked why I haven't used the new headphones. Okay. I'm Leela, and here's the story. Last month in the hostel common room, Ritika laughed at my presentation in front of everyone. She said, "Village-school English strikes again." People laughed. I went to my room and cried.

Two days later there's a box on my bed. Expensive headphones, the noise-cancelling kind, with a note: "Friends?" And Ritika smiling at me in the corridor as if nothing happened.

And I felt... wiped. As if the box were an eraser.

So I went to her room and said, gently, "Thank you, but I can't take these. What you said really hurt. I'd rather we talk about that than have headphones." She went red. We talked for an hour. I gave the box back. That talk was worth more.

Ujjwal, you're angry that Siddharth bought you a jacket instead of apologising? Let your Vijay chacha tell you about Prakash. We were twenty, both engineering students in Pune. At a party, full of his own cleverness, Prakash told everyone I'd only got in because of my uncle. I laughed it off. Inside, I was burning.

The next week he turned up with a watch. A real one, steel, very expensive. "Bhai, for you," he said, grinning, as if the party had never happened.

I wore it for three days and felt worse each day. As if I had been bought.

Then I went to his room and put the watch on his desk. "Prakash, I'm grateful. But what you said hurt. I'd rather talk than wear this." He sat down. That talk saved our friendship. He's still my closest friend. The watch? He gave it to his father.

I'm Pallavi, and last winter I missed the brochure deadline for our biggest client at the design studio. One day late. The client printed without us, and our boss had to call and apologise.

For the next month I became a machine. First in, last out. I redid old files nobody asked about. When Anjali offered to take the Diwali ads off my plate, I said, "No, I've got it," and stayed till midnight. I ate biscuits for dinner at my desk. I stopped going to my Sunday dance class.

It didn't feel like work. It felt like paying a fine.

One Friday I fell asleep on the bus and missed my stop by forty minutes. Sitting at the depot, I finally thought: I said sorry, I fixed the process. Anjali could have helped all along. The next Monday I gave her the Diwali ads.

Three weeks ago Tenzin missed the customs filing deadline for the Siliguri shipment. It cost us a day's delay. Tenzin told the client himself and fixed the filing that afternoon. That was good ownership.

Since then, though, he has logged in at seven and left after ten every day. He redid last quarter's files without being asked. When Karan offered to take the weekend report, Tenzin said, "No, I have to make up for it." He looks exhausted, and on Friday he made two small errors in forms he usually does perfectly.

Today I told him directly: "The mistake is paid for. You owned it. This extra isn't fixing anything now; it's wearing you out." I've asked Karan to take the weekend report and asked Tenzin to leave by six this week. We'll review the checklist together on Monday.

Simran
